## Intro

Getting from a corrected embedding to cell type labels involves more choices
than a single `find_clusters_sc()` call suggests. Which graph do you cluster
on? Leiden or Louvain, and how many iterations? Do you cluster every cell, or
coarsen first because you have a million of them? Do you stamp one label per
cluster, or score each cell? And once you have a well annotated data set, how
do you avoid redoing all of it every time a new sample lands on your desk?

This vignette goes through these decisions in that order:

1. Build a reference from two PBMC data sets (pbmc3k + pbmc4k), corrected
   with Harmony v2.
2. Compare the three neighbour graphs bixverse can build (sNN, the UMAP fuzzy
   simplicial set and the plain kNN union) and what they do to the clustering.
3. Leiden vs Louvain, and the fast clustering via k-means coarsening.
4. Annotate with scType, per cluster and per cell.
5. Compress the reference with Symphony
   ([Kang, et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-25957-x)), map a
   third PBMC data set (pbmc8k) into it and transfer the labels.

If you have not read the
[batch correction vignette](https://gregorlueg.github.io/bixverse/articles/single_cell_batch_corrections.html)
and the
[introductory vignette](https://gregorlueg.github.io/bixverse/articles/thinking_single_cell.html),
please do so first; this vignette assumes familiarity with both.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(bixverse)
library(bixverse.plots)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
library(magrittr)
```

## Building the reference data

### Loading the reference batches

We use the same pbmc3k + pbmc4k pair as in the batch correction vignette. Two
batches with the same broad cell type composition and a clear technical
difference between them is exactly the situation Symphony is designed for:
the reference learns the batch correction once, and that correction can then
be applied to future queries without rerunning Harmony.

```{r}
#| label: load reference
#| code-fold: true
dir_data <- download_pbmc_batches()

tempdir_ref <- file.path(tempdir(), "symphony_ref")
dir.create(tempdir_ref, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

h5ad_files <- list.files(dir_data)
h5ad_files <- h5ad_files[grepl(".h5ad", h5ad_files)]
h5ad_paths <- file.path(dir_data, h5ad_files)
names(h5ad_paths) <- c("pbmc3k", "pbmc4k")

h5_tasks <- prescan_h5ad_files(h5_paths = h5ad_paths)

sc_ref <- SingleCells(dir_data = tempdir_ref)

sc_ref <- load_multi_h5ad(
  object = sc_ref,
  prescan_result = h5_tasks,
  .verbose = TRUE
)
```

### Quality control

Standard QC: mitochondrial gene proportions, library complexity, MAD-based
outlier detection.

```{r}
#| label: reference qc
#| code-fold: true
var_ref <- get_sc_var(sc_ref)

# let's get the gene symbols from one of the h5ad files - in multi file import
# additional columns are dropped from the vars
h5_metadata <- read_h5ad_metadata(h5ad_paths[[1]])

var_ref <- merge(
  var_ref,
  h5_metadata$var[, c("ENSEMBL_ID", "Symbol_TENx")],
  by.x = "gene_id",
  by.y = "ENSEMBL_ID"
)

setnames(var_ref, old = "Symbol_TENx", new = "gene_symbol", skip_absent = TRUE)

gs_of_interest <- list(
  MT = var_ref[grepl("^MT-", gene_symbol), gene_id],
  Ribo = var_ref[grepl("^RPS|^RPL", gene_symbol), gene_id]
)

sc_ref <- gene_set_proportions_sc(
  sc_ref,
  gs_of_interest,
  streaming = FALSE,
  .verbose = TRUE
)

qc_df <- sc_ref[[c("cell_id", "lib_size", "nnz", "MT", "exp_id")]]

metrics <- list(
  log10_lib_size = log10(qc_df$lib_size),
  log10_nnz = log10(qc_df$nnz),
  MT = qc_df$MT
)
directions <- c(
  log10_lib_size = "twosided",
  log10_nnz = "twosided",
  MT = "above"
)

qc <- run_cell_qc(
  metrics = metrics,
  cells_to_keep = get_cells_to_keep(sc_ref),
  directions = directions,
  threshold = 3
)

sc_ref[["outlier"]] <- qc$combined
cells_to_keep <- qc_df[!qc$combined, cell_id]
sc_ref <- set_cells_to_keep(sc_ref, cells_to_keep)
```

### HVGs, PCA, Harmony v2

This block is the Harmony v2 path of the batch correction vignette: pick HVGs,
run PCA, run Harmony v2. Version 1 is still available via `harmony_sc()` and
`params_sc_harmony()`, but v2 is preferable in most settings (see the batch
correction vignette for the reasoning).

```{r}
#| label: reference preprocessing
sc_ref <- find_hvg_sc(
  object = sc_ref,
  hvg_no = 2000L,
  .verbose = TRUE
)

sc_ref <- calculate_pca_sc(
  object = sc_ref,
  no_pcs = 30L
)

sc_ref <- harmony_v2_sc(
  object = sc_ref,
  batch_column = "exp_id",
  harmony_params = params_sc_harmony_v2()
)
```

## Which graph to cluster on

`find_neighbours_sc()` does two things: it finds the kNN on the embedding and
it symmetrises that kNN into the undirected, weighted graph the clustering runs
on. The second step is controlled by `knn_sym` in `params_knn_graph_defaults()`,
passed via `graph` in `params_sc_neighbours()`. Three options:

- `"snn"` (default): the shared nearest neighbour graph of bluster/Seurat. Two
  cells are linked if their neighbourhoods overlap, weighted by Jaccard (or
  rank), and weak edges below `pruning` are dropped.
- `"umap"`: the fuzzy simplicial set from UMAP, i.e. what ScanPy stores in
  `obsp/connectivities`. Use this if you want your Leiden clusters to line up
  with a ScanPy pipeline.
- `"knn"`: the plain union of the kNN, every edge weighted 1.

Let's build all three on the Harmony embedding and cluster each across a few
resolutions. Every call recomputes the kNN as well, which at ~7k cells costs
nothing.

```{r}
#| label: graph comparison
graph_types <- c("snn", "umap", "knn")
resolutions <- c(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2)

n_clusters <- purrr::map(graph_types, \(graph_type) {
  sc_ref <- find_neighbours_sc(
    object = sc_ref,
    embd_to_use = "harmony_v2",
    neighbours_params = params_sc_neighbours(
      graph = list(knn_sym = graph_type)
    ),
    .verbose = FALSE
  )

  purrr::map(resolutions, \(res) {
    col_name <- sprintf("leiden_%s_%s", graph_type, res)
    sc_ref <- find_clusters_sc(sc_ref, res = res, name = col_name)
    data.table(
      graph = graph_type,
      resolution = res,
      n_clusters = uniqueN(unlist(sc_ref[[col_name]]))
    )
  }) %>%
    rbindlist()
}) %>%
  rbindlist()

dcast(n_clusters, resolution ~ graph, value.var = "n_clusters")
```

The point of this table: **resolutions do not carry over between graphs**. The
`"umap"` and `"knn"` graphs only hold the kNN pairs, while the sNN graph also
links cells that merely share neighbours and prunes weak edges. On this data
the differences are a handful of communities at a given resolution, and not
always in the same direction. On other data they can be larger. If you move a
ScanPy pipeline over and switch to `knn_sym = "umap"`, keep its resolution; if
you switch to sNN, retune it.

For the rest of the vignette we work on the sNN graph.

```{r}
#| label: reference neighbours
sc_ref <- find_neighbours_sc(
  object = sc_ref,
  embd_to_use = "harmony_v2",
  neighbours_params = params_sc_neighbours()
)

sc_ref <- umap_sc(
  sc_ref,
  slot_name = "umap_harm_v2",
  use_knn = TRUE
)
```

## Clustering

### Leiden vs Louvain

Both run in Rust, and the labels depend on `seed` only, not on the global RNG
or the number of threads. Leiden is the default; it guarantees connected
communities, which Louvain does not
([Traag, et al., 2019](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-019-41695-z)).
Labels are 0-based with `0` being the largest cluster.

```{r}
#| label: leiden and louvain
sc_ref <- find_clusters_sc(sc_ref, res = 1, name = "leiden_clusters")

sc_ref <- find_clusters_sc(
  sc_ref,
  cluster_algorithm = "louvain",
  res = 1,
  name = "louvain_clusters"
)
```

A few knobs get passed through `...` to `leiden_clustering()`:

- `n_iterations`: defaults to `2L` for Louvain and `5L` for Leiden. A negative
  value iterates until the partition is stable.
- `min_gain`: with a negative `n_iterations`, also stop once an iteration gains
  no more than this in modularity.
- `local_moving`: `"queue"` is Traag's sequential queue, `"coloured"` moves the
  nodes of one colour class in parallel. The latter only kicks in on the
  larger levels of the graph, so on 7k cells don't expect much.

```{r}
#| label: leiden until stable
sc_ref <- find_clusters_sc(
  sc_ref,
  res = 1,
  name = "leiden_stable",
  n_iterations = -1L,
  min_gain = 1e-4,
  local_moving = "coloured"
)
```

How much do the three labelings agree? A small helper that plots, for each
cluster of one labeling, how its cells spread across the clusters of another:

```{r}
#| label: overlap helper
plot_overlap <- function(a, b, name_a, name_b) {
  dt <- data.table(a = factor(a), b = factor(b))[, .N, by = .(a, b)] %>%
    .[, frac := N / sum(N), by = a]

  ggplot(dt, aes(x = b, y = a, fill = frac)) +
    geom_tile() +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(x = name_b, y = name_a, fill = "Fraction:") +
    theme_minimal()
}
```

```{r}
#| label: leiden vs louvain
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
clusters_dt <- sc_ref[[c(
  "leiden_clusters",
  "louvain_clusters",
  "leiden_stable"
)]]

plot_overlap(
  clusters_dt$leiden_clusters,
  clusters_dt$louvain_clusters,
  "Leiden",
  "Louvain"
) +
  ggtitle("Leiden vs Louvain (res = 1)")
```

```{r}
#| label: leiden vs leiden stable
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
plot_overlap(
  clusters_dt$leiden_clusters,
  clusters_dt$leiden_stable,
  "Leiden (5 iterations)",
  "Leiden (until stable)"
) +
  ggtitle("Fixed iterations vs iterating until stable")
```

### Fast clustering

On a few thousand cells the full graph clustering is instant. On a million it
isn't. `fast_cluster_sc()` coarsens the cells with k-means first (`sqrt(N)`
centroids by default), builds a graph over the centroids and runs Louvain or
Leiden on that. Each cell inherits the community of its centroid. Two options
for the centroid graph:

- the default, a symmetrised kNN between the centroids (`centroid_k`,
  `centroid_graph`);
- `cell_mediated = TRUE`, the Secuer graph
  (Wei, et al., PLoS Comput Biol, 2022), where
  each cell links its `n_anchors` nearest centroids, so two centroids are
  connected if they share cells.

With `n_seeds > 1` every resolution is run once per seed. The labels of the
seed with the lowest mean conductance are kept, and the ARI and conductance
across seeds come back as stability statistics.

```{r}
#| label: fast clustering
fc_resolutions <- c(2, 1.5, 1, 0.5)

fc_knn <- fast_cluster_sc(
  object = sc_ref,
  embd_to_use = "harmony_v2",
  resolutions = fc_resolutions,
  n_seeds = 10L
)

fc_cell_med <- fast_cluster_sc(
  object = sc_ref,
  embd_to_use = "harmony_v2",
  resolutions = fc_resolutions,
  fc_params = params_sc_fast_cluster(cell_mediated = TRUE),
  n_seeds = 10L
)
```

The stats help to pick a resolution: high ARI means the partition barely
changes between seeds, low conductance means the communities are well
separated in the centroid graph.

```{r}
#| label: fast clustering stats
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
fc_stats <- rbindlist(list(
  fc_knn$stats[, graph := "centroid kNN"],
  fc_cell_med$stats[, graph := "cell-mediated"]
))

fc_stats

melt(
  fc_stats,
  id.vars = c("graph", "resolution"),
  measure.vars = c("mean_ari", "mean_conductance")
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = resolution, y = value, colour = graph)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Resolution", y = NULL, colour = "Centroid graph:") +
  theme_minimal()
```

And how does the coarsened version compare against Leiden on the full graph?

```{r}
#| label: fast vs full
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
sc_ref <- add_sc_new_obs(
  object = sc_ref,
  obs_data = get_data(fc_cell_med)
)

fast_dt <- sc_ref[[c("leiden_clusters", "res_1")]]

plot_overlap(
  fast_dt$leiden_clusters,
  fast_dt$res_1,
  "Leiden (full graph)",
  "Fast clustering (cell-mediated, res = 1)"
) +
  ggtitle("Full vs fast clustering")
```

With ~5.8k cells there are only ~76 centroids, so the partitions come out
coarse: about 5 communities at resolution 1 against 14 for Leiden on the full
graph. For data sets of this size, stick with `find_clusters_sc()`. The fast
path earns its keep once you are in the hundreds of thousands of cells, see the
[1 million cells vignette](https://gregorlueg.github.io/bixverse/articles/single_cell_big_data.html).

## Cell type annotation

### scType per cluster

We annotate with scType
(Ianevski, et al., Nat Comm, 2022) using a
PBMC marker set.

```{r}
#| label: marker set
cell_markers <- c(
  CD3D = "T cells",
  CD3E = "T cells",
  CD3G = "T cells",
  IL7R = "CD4+ T",
  CD4 = "CD4+ T",
  CD8A = "CD8+ T",
  CD8B = "CD8+ T",
  MS4A1 = "B cells",
  CD79A = "B cells",
  CD19 = "B cells",
  CD14 = "CD14+ Mono",
  LYZ = "CD14+ Mono",
  S100A8 = "CD14+ Mono",
  FCGR3A = "CD16+ Mono",
  CDKN1C = "CD16+ Mono",
  GNLY = "NK",
  NKG7 = "NK",
  NCAM1 = "NK",
  FCER1A = "mDC",
  CD1C = "mDC",
  LILRA4 = "pDC",
  CLEC4C = "pDC",
  PPBP = "Platelet",
  PF4 = "Platelet"
)
```

`calc_sc_type_scores()` scores every cell against every marker set,
`score_clusters()` sums the scores per cluster and assigns the winner.

```{r}
#| label: sctype
cell_markers_dt <- stack(cell_markers) %>%
  as.data.table() %>%
  setnames(., c("values", "ind"), c("cell_type", "gene_symbol")) %>%
  .[, gene_symbol := as.character(gene_symbol)] %>%
  .[, gene_id := var_ref$gene_id[match(gene_symbol, var_ref$gene_symbol)]] %>%
  .[!is.na(gene_id), ]

marker_list <- prepare_cell_markers(sc_ref, cell_markers_dt)

sctype_scores <- calc_sc_type_scores(
  object = sc_ref,
  cell_marker_list = marker_list
)

cell_type_anno <- score_clusters(
  sctype_scores,
  sc_ref[[]][["leiden_clusters"]]
)

obs <- get_sc_obs(sc_ref, filtered = TRUE)[, .(
  cell_idx,
  leiden_clusters
)] %>%
  .[,
    sc_type := cell_type_anno$cell_type[match(
      leiden_clusters,
      cell_type_anno$cluster_id
    )]
  ]

sc_ref[["sc_type"]] <- obs$sc_type
```

### scType per cell

The cluster level call stamps one label on every cell of a cluster. A small
population that shares a Leiden community with a bigger one gets absorbed and
nothing flags it. `assign_sc_type()` scores per cell instead: the score matrix
is smoothed over the neighbour graph via label spreading
(Zhou, et al., NIPS, 2004),
then each cell takes its own argmax. Cells whose best score falls below
`score_floor` come back as `NA`. Pass `cluster_col` and you also get the
per-cluster composition and a hybrid call: clusters at or above
`purity_threshold` keep the cluster level label, mixed clusters fall back to
the per-cell calls.

```{r}
#| label: sctype per cell
sctype_cells <- assign_sc_type(
  object = sc_ref,
  sc_type_res = sctype_scores,
  cluster_col = "leiden_clusters",
  sctype_cell_params = params_sctype_cells()
)

sctype_cells

sc_ref[[c("sc_type_cell", "sc_type_hybrid", "sc_type_margin")]] <- list(
  sc_type_cell = sctype_cells$assignments,
  sc_type_hybrid = sctype_cells$hybrid,
  sc_type_margin = sctype_cells$margins
)
```

The composition table is the place to look for clusters that hide more than
one cell type:

```{r}
#| label: sctype composition
sctype_cells$composition
```

Most of the mixed clusters are T cell clusters split between `"T cells"` and
`"CD4+ T"` or `"CD8+ T"`. That is the marker set, not the method: the generic
`"T cells"` set (CD3D/E/G) competes with the subtype sets on the same cells. A
hierarchical marker set, or dropping the generic T cell entry, cleans this up.

The margin (best minus second best score) flags ambiguous calls:

```{r}
#| label: sctype margin plot
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
embedding_plot_sc(
  sc_ref,
  embedding = "umap_harm_v2",
  colour_by = "sc_type_margin",
  discrete = FALSE
) +
  labs(
    title = "Per-cell scType margin",
    colour = "Margin:"
  )
```

Batches mixed, cell types separated:

```{r}
#| label: reference celltype plot

#| fig-width: 7

```

And the canonical markers:

```{r}
#| label: check expression patterns - reference
feature_plot_sc(
  object = sc_ref,
  features = c(
    "ENSG00000167286",
    "ENSG00000153563",
    "ENSG00000177455",
    "ENSG00000170458"
  ),
  feature_labels = c(
    "ENSG00000167286" = "CD3D",
    "ENSG00000153563" = "CD8A",
    "ENSG00000177455" = "CD19",
    "ENSG00000170458" = "CD14"
  ),
  embedding = "umap_harm_v2"
)
```

## Reference mapping with Symphony

Once you have a well annotated reference, you don't want to redo QC, HVG
selection, PCA, batch correction, clustering and manual annotation for every
new sample. Symphony compresses the reference into a small set of cached terms
that map new query cells into the same coordinate system in a single shot, with
no need to keep the reference cells around at query time.

### Compressing into a SymphonyReference

`build_symphony_ref()` re-runs PCA and Harmony internally using the supplied
HVGs, then caches the loadings, centroids and compression terms (`Nr`, `C`)
needed for query mapping. Pass `label_columns` to snapshot one or more obs
columns, here both scType annotations, into the reference for downstream label
transfer.

A note on the apparent duplication: yes, PCA + Harmony are run again inside
`build_symphony_ref()`, even though we just ran them on the same HVGs above.
This is deliberate. The standard pipeline keeps its embeddings on the
`SingleCells` object and streams from disk; the Symphony reference keeps a
self-contained, in-memory copy of everything it needs to project queries
without the reference cells. Sharing state across those two representations
would tie them together in unhelpful ways. The cost is one extra PCA + Harmony
run at build time.

```{r}
#| label: build symphony ref
# needs +1L because 0-indexed HVGs are returned
hvg_indices <- get_hvg(sc_ref) + 1L

symphony_ref <- build_symphony_ref(
  object = sc_ref,
  batch_column = "exp_id",
  hvg = hvg_indices,
  harmony_params = params_sc_harmony_v2(),
  pca_params = params_sc_pca(),
  no_pcs = 30L,
  label_columns = c("sc_type", "sc_type_hybrid"),
  .verbose = TRUE
)

symphony_ref
```

The print method tells you the Harmony backend, the size of the loadings
and centroid matrices, the batch variables and the stored label columns.

### Loading the query

We use pbmc8k as the query. Same tissue, same broad biology, but a different
10x run: exactly the kind of "another sample arrives" scenario Symphony is
built for.

```{r}
#| label: load query
#| code-fold: true
pbmc8k_path <- download_pbmc8k()

tempdir_query <- file.path(tempdir(), "symphony_query")
dir.create(tempdir_query, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

mtx_io_params <- get_cell_ranger_params(pbmc8k_path)

sc_query <- SingleCells(dir_data = tempdir_query)

sc_query <- load_mtx(
  object = sc_query,
  sc_mtx_io_param = mtx_io_params,
  mtx_streaming = FALSE,
  .verbose = TRUE
)
```

### Quality control on the query

Same QC as the reference. We are not trying to match library sizes or anything
fancy across data sets, just remove clearly bad cells.

```{r}
#| label: query qc
#| code-fold: true
var_q <- get_sc_var(sc_query)

gs_q <- list(
  MT = var_q[grepl("^MT-", column1), gene_id],
  Ribo = var_q[grepl("^RPS|^RPL", column1), gene_id]
)

sc_query <- gene_set_proportions_sc(
  sc_query,
  gs_q,
  streaming = FALSE,
  .verbose = TRUE
)

qc_df_q <- sc_query[[c("cell_id", "lib_size", "nnz", "MT")]]

metrics_q <- list(
  log10_lib_size = log10(qc_df_q$lib_size),
  log10_nnz = log10(qc_df_q$nnz),
  MT = qc_df_q$MT
)

qc_q <- run_cell_qc(
  metrics = metrics_q,
  cells_to_keep = get_cells_to_keep(sc_query),
  directions = c(
    log10_lib_size = "twosided",
    log10_nnz = "twosided",
    MT = "above"
  ),
  threshold = 3
)

sc_query[["outlier"]] <- qc_q$combined
sc_query <- set_cells_to_keep(
  sc_query,
  qc_df_q[!qc_q$combined, cell_id]
)
```

### Projecting the query

`map_symphony_query()` does the actual projection: query cells are
standardised against the reference's per-HVG means and SDs, projected through
the reference PCA loadings, and assigned soft cluster weights against the
reference centroids. Those weights then drive the cached MoE batch correction,
putting query cells into the same `z_corr` coordinate system as the reference.

Genes are matched by name. Missing HVGs are treated as zero columns; the
function reports how many were missing.

pbmc8k is a single batch, so we pass `batch_column = NULL`, which skips the
query-side correction (the resulting `symphony` embedding then equals
`symphony_pca`). With several query batches, pass the batch column and
Symphony corrects them against the reference.

```{r}
#| label: map query
sc_query <- map_symphony_query(
  reference = symphony_ref,
  query = sc_query,
  batch_column = NULL,
  params = params_symphony_map(),
  .verbose = TRUE
)
```

The query now carries three embeddings: `"symphony"` (z_corr, the corrected
embedding), `"symphony_pca"` (z_pca, pre-correction), and `"symphony_r"`
(soft cluster assignments, one column per reference centroid).

A neighbour graph and UMAP on the corrected embedding give us something to
plot against:

```{r}
#| label: query umap
sc_query <- find_neighbours_sc(
  object = sc_query,
  embd_to_use = "symphony",
  neighbours_params = params_sc_neighbours()
)

sc_query <- umap_sc(
  sc_query,
  embd_to_use = "symphony",
  slot_name = "umap_symphony",
  use_knn = TRUE
)
```

### Transferring labels

`transfer_labels_symphony()` does a kNN majority vote on the reference's
`z_corr` (the searchable index) using the query's `"symphony"` embedding. It
reads labels from the reference's stored `labels` slot, the one we populated
via `label_columns` at build time. Distances on `z_corr` are Euclidean; the
default `params_sc_knn()` matches.

```{r}
#| label: transfer labels
predicted <- transfer_labels_symphony(
  reference = symphony_ref,
  query = sc_query,
  label_column = "sc_type_hybrid",
  knn_params = params_sc_knn(),
  .verbose = TRUE
)

head(predicted)
```

The result is a `data.table` in `get_cells_to_keep(query)` order with a
predicted label and a confidence score (fraction of neighbours agreeing on
the winning class). We can attach both directly to the query obs.

```{r}
#| label: attach predictions
sc_query[[c(
  "predicted_sc_type",
  "sc_type_confidence"
)]] <- list(
  predicted_sc_type = predicted$predicted_sc_type_hybrid,
  sc_type_confidence = predicted$confidence_sc_type_hybrid
)
```

### Visualising the result

Query UMAP coloured by transferred cell type:

```{r}
#| label: query celltype plot
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
embedding_plot_sc(
  sc_query,
  embedding = "umap_symphony",
  colour_by = "predicted_sc_type",
  label_by = "predicted_sc_type",
  discrete = TRUE
) +
  labs(
    title = "pbmc8k - transferred cell types",
    colour = "Cell type:"
  )
```

Same UMAP, coloured by transfer confidence. Cells in the interior of their
cell type sit at confidence 1; cells on cluster boundaries or in cell types
poorly represented in the reference are the ones to scrutinise.

```{r}
#| label: query confidence plot
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
embedding_plot_sc(
  sc_query,
  embedding = "umap_symphony",
  colour_by = "sc_type_confidence",
  discrete = FALSE
) +
  labs(
    title = "pbmc8k - kNN transfer confidence",
    colour = "Confidence:"
  )
```

And a per-cell-type confidence distribution, useful for spotting cell types
where the reference and query disagree systematically:

```{r}
#| label: confidence boxplot
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
conf_dt <- sc_query[[c("predicted_sc_type", "sc_type_confidence")]]

ggplot(conf_dt, aes(x = predicted_sc_type, y = sc_type_confidence)) +
  geom_violin(scale = "width", fill = "grey80") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.2, size = 0.4) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Transfer confidence",
    title = "Per-cell-type kNN agreement on pbmc8k"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)) +
  ylim(0, 1.025)
```

Sanity check of the transferred labels with the canonical markers:

```{r}
#| label: check expression patterns - query
feature_plot_sc(
  object = sc_query,
  features = c(
    "ENSG00000167286",
    "ENSG00000153563",
    "ENSG00000177455",
    "ENSG00000170458"
  ),
  feature_labels = c(
    "ENSG00000167286" = "CD3D",
    "ENSG00000153563" = "CD8A",
    "ENSG00000177455" = "CD19",
    "ENSG00000170458" = "CD14"
  ),
  embedding = "umap_symphony"
)
```

### Slim references and post-hoc labels

The reference above stores `z_corr`, `z_orig`, the soft cluster assignments
`r` and the labels. For large references that get checked into shared
storage, `z_orig` and `r` are dead weight; passing `slim = TRUE` at build time
drops them. `z_corr` is always retained, since kNN label transfer searches
against it.

If you want to add or update labels after the reference is built (say, you
re-ran scType with a different marker set), use `add_symphony_labels()`. It
reads obs columns from a `SingleCells` object in `cells_to_keep` order and
snapshots them into the reference. The `cells_to_keep` state must match the
reference; the function errors if the row count drifts.

```{r}
#| label: slim plus add labels
#| eval: false
slim_ref <- build_symphony_ref(
  object = sc_ref,
  batch_column = "exp_id",
  hvg = hvg_indices,
  harmony_params = params_sc_harmony_v2(),
  pca_params = params_sc_pca(),
  no_pcs = 30L,
  slim = TRUE
)

slim_ref <- add_symphony_labels(
  reference = slim_ref,
  sc_object = sc_ref,
  columns = "sc_type"
)
```

Multiple label columns can be attached at once (`columns = c(...)`), existing
columns are protected unless you pass `overwrite = TRUE`, and
`get_symphony_labels(reference)` returns the stored `data.table` (or `NULL` if
none).

## Clean up

```{r}
#| label: clean up
unlink(tempdir_ref, recursive = TRUE, force = TRUE)
unlink(tempdir_query, recursive = TRUE, force = TRUE)
```
